Released at:   30 April 2026
Table number:   39
Table name:  Key terms and definitions
The following key terms are used throughout the AusPlay survey (AusPlay) reporting and other collateral, and a definition is provided for each of them below in alphabetical order.
Adult
For the purposes of AusPlay an adult is a person aged 15 and over. To be eligible to complete the survey, the individual must also have lived in Australia for the  at least the last 12 months.
Barriers

Non-participants (those who had not participated in any sport or physical activities during the past 12 months) are asked about the reasons why they had not done so.  Respondents are able to choose from a list of potential reasons, in addition to an 'other' category. Multiple responses are allowed. This question is asked both of adults and, by proxy, of children (with the parent responding on behalf of the child).
Child

For the purposes of AusPlay a child is a person aged 0-14. Responding adults aged 18 and over are asked whether they are a parent or guardian to a child aged under 15 who lived in the same household. Where there is more than one child, a random selection is done using the last birthday method; i.e. the respondent is directed to report on the child aged 0-14 who most recently had a birthday. The responding adult then answers questions about the selected child’s participation in organised sport or physical activity outside of school hours on the child's behalf.
Disability

Respondents aged 18+ are asked if they have a disability or physical condtion that restricts their life in some way. If they say 'yes' they are categorised as having a disability, regardless of how long it has lasted or is likely to last.
Duration

Those who say they did at least one sport or physical activity in the past 12 months are asked follow up questions about each activity they did. For each activity done within the last 12 months, all respondents are asked how long the most recent session had lasted. Respondents are required to provide an answer in hours (0-23) and minutes (0-50 in ten minute increments). There was also an option for days (1 to 4+) to account for multi-day events.  An average duration is calculated for each person from the durations they gave for their different activities, and this is used as an indicative session duration for reporting durations per person.
Estimated number of participants

Estimated number of participants is derived by extrapolating the results from the survey to the target population and applying weights to ensure they are representative of the latest Australian Estimated Resident Population (ERP) figures published by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS). As any survey is subject to sampling error (see Relative Margin of Error below) the numbers provided in these tables are estimates only. Estimates are not rounded to the nearest thousand so that the potential for confusion caused by rounding errors is removed.
Frequency

Those who say they did at least one sport or physical activity in the past 12 months are asked follow questions about each activity they did. For each activity done within the last 12 months, all respondents are how many times, in total, they did each activity (including any practice or training). The frequencies given by each person for each of their activities are summed for reporting the total frequency of participation in any sport-related or non-sport-related activities per person.
Informal activity
Refers to an activity that is self-organised and is carried out either alone or with friends/family on a casual basis.
Motivation

All adult respondents who say they did at least one sport or physical activity in the past 12 months are asked their reasons for participating in those activities. Respondents are able to choose from a list of potential motivations, in addition to an 'other' category.  Multiple responses are allowed.

Because motivation data was activity specific, to report people’s motivations for participation generally, the motivations each person provides are combined, recording when a particular motivation is mentioned for at least one of the person’s activities. This captures the full range of motivations a person provides for participating, while avoiding double-counting cases when the same motivation is mentioned by one person for different activities.
Non-participant (adult)
All adults say they had not participated in any physical activity for sport, recreation or exercise, during the last 12 months, are referred to as non-participants.
Non-participant (children)
All children who are reported to have not participated in organised sport or physical activity, outside of school hours, during the last 12 months are referred to as ‘non-participants’.
Non-player involvement

Adult respondents are asked whether they had been involved with any sports in a non-playing role, such as an official, coach, referee or administrator in the last 12 months. Those who had are referred to as ‘adults involved as non-players’.
Number of activities

Up to ten separate activities (at the output level) could be recorded for each adult and child respondent. The number of activities is the sum of each individual’s total number of separate activities (at the output level) played during the last 12 months.
Organisation of activity

For each activity recorded, respondents are asked about the different ways that they had done each activity, directing respondents to indicate whether they had done the activity through an organisation and/or informally by themselves or with friends. Respondents are able to choose from a list of potential options, in addition to an 'other' category. Multiple responses are allowed. For adults, the list of options to choose from includes a range of entities often involved in delivering 'organised' sport and physical activities (eg. sports associations, commercial businesses), as well as options that indicate the activity was informally organised (ie. the activity was done alone by the respondent, with friends, or without a formal organising body involved).  For children, given only data about participation in organised sports outside of school hours is collected, the list of options to choose from is limited to entities often involved in delivering 'organised' sport.
Location/venue of activity

For each recorded activity, respondents are asked about where they had done each activity, directing respondents to indicate whether they had done the activity at a specific type of venue (eg. sports club, community centre) and/or location (eg. public space, work, home). Respondents are able to choose from a list of potential options, in addition to an 'other' category. Multiple responses are allowed.
Organised activity

Refers to an activity that is carried out on a formal or semi-formal basis, organised by an entity such as a sports or recreation club/association, a gym/fitness club/sports/aquatic centre, a private or commercial business, a personal trainer/coach, an event, work, educational institution, community organisation or social group.
Participant
See ‘Player (adult)’ and ‘Player (child)’.
Participation by adults

All adults (aged 15 and over) are asked whether they had participated in any physical activities for sport, for exercise, or for recreation in the last 12 months. Further information about types of activities that are in and out of scope are provided to the respondent in short, dot point form.  Up to ten separate activities can  be recorded and subsequent questions are  then asked about  each activity (frequency, duration, whether organised or informal, where it took place, cost  and motivations).
Participation by children

Among children, participation is limited to activities done outside of school hours (since parents often do not know accurately what activities are done within school), and to organised activities (sport or physical activity) (since non-organised activity is difficult for parents to accurately define and quantify among children). The responding parent/guardian answers on behalf of a randomly selected child aged 0-14 in their household.  As with adults, a maximum of 10 activities can be recorded. Activities are coded in the same way as  for adults.
Participation rate
The participation rate indicates the proportion of the adult or child population who participated in at least one sport or physical activity in the past 12 months.
Payment

For each recorded activity, respondents are asked about the approximate total cost paid to take part in the activity over the past 12 months. It includes all costs of registration or membership paid to an organisation and costs paid to access specific venues, but does not include other costs such as equipment, clothing etc).
Player (adult)

Adult respondents who say they had participated in some form of sport or physical activity during the last 12 months are called ‘players’, for ease of reference. Those who had not participated, during the last 12 months, are referred to as ‘non-participants’.
Player (child)

Children who are reported to have participated in some form of organised physical activity outside of school hours in the last 12 months are called ‘players’, for ease of reference. Those who had not participated, during the last 12 months, are referred to as ‘non-participants’.

Among children, participation is limited to activities done outside of school hours (since parents often do not know accurately what activities are done within school), and to organised activities (sport or physical activity) (since non-organised activity is difficult for parents to accurately define and quantify among children).

The responding parent/guardian answered on behalf of a randomly selected child in their household.  They are asked about what organised sports or physical activities the child had participated in outside of school hours in the last 12 months.  Further information about types of activities that are in and out of scope are provided to the respondent in short, dot point form.
Relative margin of error (RMOE)

All survey data generated from a sample of a given population has a margin of error (MoE) associated with it. The margin of error refers to the amount of random sampling error in the survey responses in absolute terms (ie.  difference in number of people), or as a percentage of the absolute or true result (ie. % variation in the number of people - this is referred to as the relative margin of error (RMoE)). The relative margin of error (RMoE) provides an indication of the precision or reliability of a given estimate. The smaller the relative margin of error, the more confident one can be that the given estimate would closely represent the true incidence in the population, should a census be conducted.

These statistical principles are based on a range of assumptions about the underlying sample.  Technically an online panel survey is known as a 'non-probability sample' and does not meet all these assumptions.  However, these concepts remain useful to assist users interpret the reliability of the survey results in practice, and noting this caveat indicative MoE and RMoE figures are still provided for AusPlay users.
Sport-related activity

AusPlay captures a wide variety of activities (see ‘Participation by adults’ and ‘Participation by children’) and a distinction in the reporting is made between sport-related activities and non-sport-related physical activities.

Sport-related activities include, for example, team sports (basketball, football, Australian football, cricket, netball, etc.), running/jogging, swimming, cycling, golf, etc. These are typically activities related to National Sporting Organisations (NSOs), although the participant may or may not play the activity through an affiliation with the NSO.
Non-sport-related physical activity

AusPlay captures a wide variety of activities (see ‘Participation by adults’ and ‘Participation by children’) and a distinction in the reporting is made between sport-related activities and non-sport related physical activities.

Non-sport-related physical activities include, for example, gym/fitness activities, bushwalking, recreational (non-sport) dance, etc. These are typically activities not related to National Sporting Organisations (NSOs).
Volunteer

Adult respondents who say they were involved in sports or physical activites as non-players in the past 12 months are asked whether they received any payment or other goods/services for their involvement. Those who received no payment  are automatically categorised as volunteers. Those who  received at least some payment or other goods/services are counted as a volunteer if they consider themselves to be volunteers when asked explicitly about this.
